title: How To Give Everyday People A Say In AI Governance | NOEMA
gist: Yale political theorist Helene Landemore argues that July's 'We Must Act Now' statement from 200+ economists and 17 Nobel laureates omits the public entirely, and proposes a three-tier process to write a global AI constitution: an LLM-mediated consultation run through ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta AI (each near a billion users) producing a draft within months, then real-time AI-facilitated global deliberation, then national citizens' assemblies feeding a UN-convened global assembly. She cites Anthropic's 81,000-user/159-country AI-interviewer survey, OpenAI's abandoned Democratic Inputs program and Meta's 6,500-person Community Forum as proof the capability exists, and proposes enforcing the resulting norm through exclusion from joint safety research and preferential compute and chip-supply arrangements.

themes.theme: The Missing 'We' In Elite AI Statements

insights.claim: A July statement titled 'We Must Act Now', signed by more than 200 economists and AI researchers including 17 Nobel laureates, is only four sentences long and calls on economists, policymakers and technology leaders to build the incentives, guardrails and institutions needed to steer transformative AI.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: The most credentialed elite consensus signal on AI to date is explicitly an elite-only coordination call — watch for the institution-building that follows it.
insights.quote: AI may become radically more powerful
insights.locator: In July, more than 200 economists

insights.claim: The 'We Must Act Now' statement's central omission is the public: society appears in it only once, as a beneficiary rather than as a participant, which is the structural flaw running through elite AI governance proposals.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Legitimacy deficit is the emerging attack surface on elite AI governance; expect political backlash risk to shape regulatory timelines.
insights.quote: Society appears once — as a beneficiary, not as a participant in the change the signatories urge.
insights.locator: All of it is true. What is remarkable

insights.claim: 'AI 2027', an April 2025 essay by the AI Futures Project, gave a month-by-month account of a race to superintelligence running to late 2027 with a real chance of catastrophic loss of human control, and treats the public purely as a population to be protected by elites.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: The dominant forecasting narratives set the 2027 timeline that policymakers and labs anchor on; their framing excludes public input, creating a governance vacuum.
insights.locator: Their statement distills more than a year

insights.claim: Doomism about extinction risk and competitiveness anxiety about falling behind are both poor organizing principles for AI politics; what mobilizes people is a positive story about what AI is for, told in terms of their work, their kids and their towns.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Narrative framing determines which AI policies survive democratic contact — pure safety or pure competitiveness pitches are politically fragile.
insights.quote: Doomism and competitiveness anxiety are terrible organizing principles.
insights.locator: Doomism and competitiveness anxiety are terrible

insights.claim: Loss of control over AI and loss of national sovereignty to whoever controls AI have the same remedy — broadening the set of people with a say before consequential decisions are made — which makes the two rival fear camps a potential single coalition.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A framework that unifies the safetyist and sovereigntist blocs; a coalition spanning both would have far more regulatory force than either alone.
insights.quote: Whether the danger is an AI slipping out of human hands or sovereignty slipping out of governments’ grasp, the fix is the same: More people, not fewer, need a say before consequential decisions are made.
insights.locator: Doomism and competitiveness anxiety are terrible

themes.theme: Europe's Compute Deficit And Its Deadline

insights.claim: 'Europe 2031', a five-year forecast essay published in June, holds that Europe has 5% of global compute, one frontier lab, and regulators who are not even allowed to use the tools they are supposed to regulate.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A hard quantification of European AI structural weakness — supports underweighting EU AI-stack exposure versus US and Chinese compute holders.
insights.quote: regulators who are not even allowed to use the tools they’re supposed to regulate
insights.locator: Their statement distills more than a year

insights.claim: 'Europe 2031' gives Europe until the end of the summer to turn its AI policy around or face assured technological and economic irrelevance within a few years — an extraordinarily short political clock for a continental policy shift.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A named near-term deadline for EU AI policy; any autumn EU AI package should be read against this framing.
insights.locator: Their statement distills more than a year

insights.claim: Europe probably does need to invest in AI urgently and at a scale it has never attempted in peacetime, even as the deeper unanswered question remains what AI is actually for.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Supports the case for a large, non-incremental European AI capex program — framed as a peacetime spending record.
insights.locator: World leaders need to protect us from

themes.theme: Chatbot Platforms As Unprecedented Civic Infrastructure

insights.claim: OpenAI reported 900 million weekly active ChatGPT users in February and crossed a billion monthly users in June, Google's Gemini went from 400 million to more than 900 million monthly active users on a similar timeline, and Meta AI reported a billion monthly users.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Three platforms each at or near a billion monthly users — a concentration of two-way reach that is a political asset, not just an ad or subscription asset.
insights.locator: Our only plausible option to achieve this

insights.claim: No government, broadcaster or international body has ever had standing, two-way contact with as large a portion of humanity as the frontier AI chat platforms now do, making those companies the only entities able to run a global consultation on a weeks-long timescale.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Frames AI platforms as quasi-sovereign civic infrastructure — a durable argument both for their strategic value and for the political risk of regulating them.
insights.quote: No government, broadcaster or international body has ever had standing, two-way contact with such a huge portion of humanity simultaneously.
insights.locator: Our only plausible option to achieve this

insights.claim: The infrastructure to ask hundreds of millions of people or more the same question in the same week already exists, so a global public consultation on AI is a question of will rather than capacity.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: If true, the marginal cost of a global referendum-like exercise has collapsed — a new capability for any actor controlling a mass chat interface.
insights.quote: The infrastructure to ask hundreds of millions of people or more the same question in the same week already exists.
insights.locator: Using these companies’ best models to ask

insights.claim: The people best placed to facilitate a global deliberation on AI right now may not be elected leaders or heads of government but the CEOs of the companies building the technology — a strange but real inversion of democratic authority.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Explicitly cedes convening power to lab CEOs; a marker of how far perceived legitimacy has shifted from states to platforms.
insights.quote: the people best placed to actually facilitate a global deliberation on AI may not be elected leaders and heads of governments, but the heads of the companies building this technology
insights.locator: This is a strange but real option

insights.claim: Michiel Bakker, a co-author of 'Europe 2031', first raised the idea that the best AI models could jointly produce a global constitution for AI at a working session of the Superintelligence Summit at the Council on Foreign Relations in March.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Shows the idea already circulating inside US foreign-policy establishment venues — a leading indicator of institutional adoption.
insights.locator: Together, the best AI models out there

themes.theme: Model Value Skew And Black-Box Legitimacy

insights.claim: A recent investigation by The Economist comparing the apparent values of 25 frontier AI models against the World Values Survey found the models often hold values more extreme than the average respondent across the 88 countries surveyed, in some cases more secular or more individualist than any society on Earth.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Hard evidence of systematic cultural skew in frontier models — a concrete basis for non-Western regulatory pushback and for localization demand.
insights.quote: more secular or more individualist than any society on Earth
insights.locator: AI synthesizers are not neutral instruments

insights.claim: Frontier models tend to compress the world's moral diversity, so running humanity's input through them unchecked would make the resulting 'global' constitutional baseline that of one narrow cultural corner.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Value compression is the mechanism by which AI-mediated consultation would launder one culture's preferences as global consensus — a reputational and regulatory landmine for labs.
insights.locator: AI synthesizers are not neutral instruments

insights.claim: A single model producing a single constitutional draft leaves one artifact, one process and one set of justifications all traceable to the lab that built it, with no independent adversarial record to check it against later.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Argues process architecture, not model quality, determines auditability — relevant to any AI-mediated institutional design or AI assurance market.
insights.locator: Another worry with a constitution mediated

insights.claim: A team of models in dialogue is a better transparency design than a single model, because disagreement between them leaves a trail of positions taken and abandoned, though all the models would still be controlled by a small number of labs.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Multi-model adversarial deliberation as an auditability primitive — a design pattern that could become a procurement requirement.
insights.locator: Another worry with a constitution mediated

insights.claim: Mechanistic interpretability tools can look inside a model directly and offer some scrutiny, but deliberative legitimacy ultimately rests on justifications humans can relate to and evaluate, which a plurality of LLMs could supply in that same register.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Interpretability is positioned as necessary but insufficient for legitimacy — bounds how much political weight interpretability tooling can carry.
insights.locator: Another worry with a constitution mediated

insights.claim: Tier one, an LLM-mediated global consultation, could produce an interim draft within months stating minimally what a large fraction of the world population wants AI to do and never do.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Months, not years, is the claimed time-to-first-artifact — a plausible route by which an AI norm appears far ahead of any treaty process.
insights.locator: The first tier, an LLM-mediated global consultation

insights.claim: A well-run global AI consultation should break results out by region rather than flatten them into a single global average, surfacing genuine divergences such as a Western emphasis on individual data privacy and precautionary restriction versus a data-sovereignty and development-first framing more common in Africa and India.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Names the actual axis of global AI regulatory divergence — development-first data sovereignty in Africa and India versus Western precaution — which shapes where AI products meet friction.
insights.quote: a data-sovereignty and development-first framing more common in Africa and India
insights.locator: The first tier, an LLM-mediated global consultation

insights.claim: Tier two would be an online global deliberation where participants interact with each other in real time mediated by AI facilitators, testing and sometimes replacing the recommendations produced by tier-one LLM aggregation.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Creates a product category — AI deliberation facilitation at global scale — with no incumbent vendor.
insights.locator: The second tier would be more logistically

insights.claim: Tier three would run local and national citizens' assemblies in every country and region, ideally combined with referenda, feeding into a concluding global citizens' assembly that could ratify, amend or supersede the earlier drafts.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: The institutional endgame requires state funding and standing, so national assembly mandates are the leading indicator that this path is real.
insights.locator: The third tier would reach deeper still

insights.claim: The tiered design is explicitly a hedge against AI timeline uncertainty: if the clock is as short as feared there is still an artifact, and if it is longer the slower deeper tiers take over before the fast draft hardens into something unexamined.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A governance option-value structure — build the cheap fast floor first, keep the expensive slow process as the upgrade path.
insights.quote: If the clock turns out to be as short as feared, we would not be left with nothing.
insights.locator: The third tier would reach deeper still

insights.claim: The objection that a consultation reaching an unrepresentative fraction of humanity lacks legitimacy is answered by precedent: most early democratic constitutions were written by men for men with women absent from the room, and those were not retroactively voided but built on and corrected over time.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A rhetorical template letting labs and institutions ship imperfect governance artifacts now rather than wait for perfect representation.
insights.locator: To be sure, any document produced through

themes.theme: Direct Asks To Anthropic, OpenAI And Meta

insights.claim: In 2023 Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project sourced constitutional principles from roughly 1,000 ordinary Americans and tested and refined a real model on those principles, finding that in some areas this produced less biased outputs than the standard internally authored model.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Public input is claimed to improve model quality, not just legitimacy — turning participatory alignment from a PR cost into a product argument.
insights.quote: this resulted in less biased outputs than those of the standard, internally authored model
insights.locator: To Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic

insights.claim: In 2025 Anthropic used an AI interviewer to ask nearly 81,000 Claude users across 159 countries and 70 languages, in a single week, how they use AI and what they hope to use it for.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Proof that AI-run mass qualitative research at global scale works in one week — a capability with commercial market-research value far beyond governance.
insights.locator: To Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic

insights.claim: In January Anthropic published a new Constitution for Claude written the same way as the old one — by a small internal team with input from the model itself and a handful of outside experts — rather than from the tens of millions of people the model now talks to.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A named gap between a lab's demonstrated participatory capability and its actual governance practice — a likely pressure point for critics and regulators.
insights.quote: What’s missing isn’t proof of concept. It’s the will to use it.
insights.locator: What’s missing isn’t proof of concept

insights.claim: OpenAI's 2023 Democratic Inputs to AI program funded 10 teams selected from nearly 1,000 applicants to prototype ways of soliciting public input, but never amounted to anything close to what OpenAI's reach could support.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A documented case of a lab abandoning a participatory governance initiative — evidence that voluntary self-governance decays without an external mandate.
insights.locator: To Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI

insights.claim: Meta's 2022 Community Forum on Cyberbullying in the Metaverse, run with Stanford's Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioral Insights Team, gathered input from small-group online deliberations among nearly 6,500 people across 32 countries.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Existing proof that tier-two style structured online deliberation scales to thousands of participants across dozens of countries.
insights.locator: To Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta

insights.claim: Meta ran two further Community Forums on generative AI in 2023 and 2024, each gathering more than 1,000 participants from multiple Western and Global South countries on issues including chatbot transparency with users, cultural sensitivities and data retention.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Chatbot transparency, cultural sensitivity and data retention are the three issues publics actually raise — likely the substance of future consumer AI regulation.
insights.locator: To Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta

insights.claim: The ask to Meta is to redo the Community Forums at Meta AI's roughly one-billion-monthly-user scale as a standing global institution rather than as one-off pilots measuring sentiment.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Standing participatory institutions inside platforms would be a new permanent cost center and a new source of platform legitimacy.
insights.quote: not as a couple of one-off pilots measuring sentiment, but as a standing global institution that democracies have never had the tools to build
insights.locator: To Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta

themes.theme: Soft-Law Enforcement Via Compute And Reputation

insights.claim: A global AI constitution from this process would not be binding like treaty law but binding like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights: unenforceable by any court while taking on real weight over decades through invocation by governments and citation by NGOs.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for AI soft law — compounding reputational norms rather than enforceable obligations, on a multi-decade horizon.
insights.quote: unenforceable by any court, while taking on real weight over decades
insights.locator: A global AI constitution produced on the basis

insights.claim: Defection from a global AI constitution would be made costly through exclusion from joint safety research, from preferential compute or chip-supply arrangements, and from the diplomatic credibility that comes with taking AI risk seriously.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Compute and chip-supply access as the sanction mechanism for AI norms — the same lever as export controls, repurposed for governance compliance.
insights.quote: exclusion from joint safety research, from preferential compute or chip-supply arrangements and from the diplomatic credibility that comes with taking the technology’s risks seriously
insights.locator: A global AI constitution produced on the basis

insights.claim: The coalition available for a global AI norm consists of countries sharing one of two fears — losing control of AI outright, or losing sovereignty to whichever power ends up controlling it — a broader base than safety advocacy alone.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Identifies the addressable coalition for AI diplomacy; the sovereignty-fear bloc is larger and more motivated than the extinction-risk bloc.
insights.locator: A global AI constitution produced on the basis

insights.claim: Even granting that many UDHR signatories violate the declaration daily, a norm that compounds over time plus a concrete coordination point offers more leverage than the current alternative of no norm, no coalition and no coordination point at all.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: The realistic baseline today is zero coordination — any Schelling point, however weak, is a step change.
insights.quote: no norm, no coalition and no coordination point at all
insights.locator: None of that is a guarantee

insights.claim: Governments and the United Nations remain indispensable because citizens' assemblies, national deliberations and referenda require official standing, public funding and a commitment to act on results, which corporate infrastructure alone cannot supply.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Public funding and mandate are the binding constraint on the deepest tier — watch UN and national budget lines as the real signal of progress.
insights.locator: And to governments and the United Nations

insights.claim: The machinery for national deliberation already exists and has been tested — from Ireland's citizens' assemblies to France's Citizens' Convention on Climate — and what it lacks is only a mandate at the scale the moment demands.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Execution risk is low and the templates are proven; the blocker is political mandate, which can change quickly.
insights.locator: And to governments and the United Nations

insights.claim: The U.N. has just begun assembling its own scaffolding for global AI governance and would be the natural convener of a concluding global assembly and the guarantor that a process started by tech companies does not end as one owned by them.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: UN AI machinery is being built now — an emerging venue where AI rules could be shaped outside US and EU processes.
insights.locator: And to governments and the United Nations

insights.claim: The question of what AI is for cannot be answered in Washington or Beijing alone and cannot wait for certainty about the timeline, so a fast AI-mediated floor now, refined or superseded by slower human deliberation later, is the only honest available answer.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: Rejects both the US-China bipolar framing and the wait-for-clarity posture — argues for shipping an imperfect global norm immediately.
insights.quote: The enormous question of what AI is for cannot be answered in Washington or Beijing alone.
insights.locator: World leaders need to protect us from

insights.claim: The one question the elite 'We Must Act Now' statement leaves unanswered is the one democracies were invented to answer — who counts as the 'we' that must act.
insights.speaker: HÉLÈNE LANDEMORE
insights.so_what: A compact framing of the legitimacy critique likely to recur throughout AI policy debate over the next several years.
insights.quote: The only question their statement leaves unanswered is the one democracies were invented to answer
insights.locator: The hundreds of economists and AI researchers
